newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Gene therapy firm offers cures, but doubts linger.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Gene therapy firm offers cures, but doubts linger.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Gene therapy promises to cure killer diseases and make fortunes for companies which bring such treatments to market.
But research is still at an early stage, and some experts say money spent on seeking remedies down this road will simply be a waste of time. Gene therapy is a blind alley, they say.
Arguments about ethics swirl around the world of gene therapy, and disputes about patenting what some people regard as human life are still raging.
In the related field of biotechnology, extravagant promises have excited investors but have so far yielded decidedly thin pickings in terms of cures and profits.
EXPECTED SCRAMBLE FOR OXFORD BIOMEDICA
Fledgling gene therapy company Oxford BioMedica Plc is being floated on the stock market on Tuesday, and investors are apparently ignoring the negatives and scrambling to get a piece of the action.
Oxford BioMedica hopes to raise about 11 million from the flotation of a 22 percent stake in the company, valuing it at 56 million.
So far it has not sold a single product.
GENE THERAPY OFFERS CURE FOR KILLER DISEASES
Not a single patient in the world has ever been cured by gene therapy.
But Professor Alan Kingsman, chief executive of Oxford Biomedica, believes gene therapy can relieve and eventually cure diseases which now can kill within a year of diagnosis.
Cures for conditions like arthritis, which, while not life threatening, cause much misery, are also on the cards.

"We plan to address the most serious life threatening diseases first -- focusing on four cancers -- ovarian, lower bowel, prostate, and glioma (brain cancer). We plan an AIDS product, a cystic fibrosis product and a Parkinson's (disease) product. All of these conditions lend themselves quite well to gene therapy as a strategy," Kingsman said in a telephone interview.

Biotechnologists manipulate living organisms such as cells or bacteria and create products which fight disease, enhance the performance of agricultural products, or induce crops to fight natural predators.
Gene therapy was developed from biotechnology's ability to isolate and manipulate genes. Normal genes are introduced into defective or missing ones to correct disorders which are often hereditary.
Kingsman said Oxford Biomedica should have its first products in clinical trials by 2000.
"Not so many years after that we should see products on the market," Kingsman said.
PATENT LAW MUST BE NAILED DOWN FIRST
Before companies like Oxford Biomedica can begin investing in research, the vexed issue of patent law must be resolved.
"Patenting is the cornerstone of the technology because it costs such a lot to develop new therapies. It is absolutely critical that they be protected by patents," Kingsman said.

The European Parliament rejected a draft law on gene therapy in March 1995, and various committees are now trying to come up with an acceptable form of words which will overcome objectors. They say a gene is a form of human life and therefore cannot be owned by companies.
Gene therapy companies hope the idea that the actual techniques of gene manipulation can be considered as different from the genes themselves will get over this point.
The European Parliament is expected to debate the issue in February or March 1997.

"Hopefully the issue will be concluded before the end of 1997, but already we can see delaying tactics beginning to be adopted by those opposed to biotechnology and gene patenting," Alastair Kent, director of the Genetic Interest Group, told a recent conference. The Genetic Interest Group seeks to promote cures for those with genetic disorders. GENE THERAPY COULD BE BLIND ALLEY
Julie Sheppard, spokeswomen for the Genetics Forum, speaks for the opposition. The Genetics Forum is a lobby group which encourages debate on the use of gene technology.
Sheppard says that far from helping to spur research, patents, by giving exclusive ownership, would be an inhibition.
And Sheppard isn't convinced research along these lines would be effective.

"We don't want to stand in the way of effective treatments, but gene therapy is a deeply flawed approach. Cancer is often behaviourally or environmentally induced. It (gene therapy) is essentially a cell killing approach which even if successful could only ever be a handmaiden to more conventional therapies based on chemotherapy or radiotherapy," Sheppard said.

"Gene therapy involves identifying genes which cause disease, isolating them, copying them then altering them, then reinserting at the right place in the genetic sequence. That's an awful lot of ifs," she continued.
Investment in biotechnology has been big on promises and short on reward, Sheppard said.

"Lots of little biotechnology companies have raised a lot of venture capital on the basis of extraordinary and extravagant claims based on new cures based on new gene therapy and production of pharmaceuticals.

"But none of these (in Europe) has actually delivered a product yet. The commercial dynamic of research scientists working within these companies has seduced them into making premature promises that can't be kept. It's happened here and in the U.S.," Sheppard said.
GENE THERAPY REMAINS UNPROVEN, EXPERIMENTAL
Even the Genetic Interest Group concedes that gene therapy has some way to go to prove itself.

"It remains true today that gene therapy is still theoretical, and in a few cases experimental. It is a long way from being the preferred form of therapy for any of a wide range of diseases which afflict us," Kent said.
Professor Kingsman remains steadfast in the hope that gene therapy can give relief to sufferers from incurable diseases.

"Just take glioma. In a large proportion of cases life expectancy is less than one year. Yes, there are very theoretical risks, but weigh that against the benefit of keeping someone alive for perhaps five years, perhaps for their natural life span," Kingsman said.

"Most people would think that's worth the theoretical risk. Clearly, if some horrendous, real risk was established one might think again, but the sorts of things we are doing have no tangible obvious risks associated with them."
